newsitem.title: USA: Murdoch's News Corp. forms alliance with EchoStar.
newsitem.headline: Murdoch's News Corp. forms alliance with EchoStar.

text.p: News Corp. Ltd., on Monday announced an alliance with EchoStar Communications Corp. DISH.O to offer a subscription television service in the United States that would compete cable providers.

According to terms of the deal, Rupert Murdoch's News Corp., the owner of the Fox television network, would contribute satellites, cash and other assets of $1 billion from its American Sky Broadcasting (AskyB) unit in return for a 50 percent stake in EchoStar.

MCI Communications Corp., which is a partner in ASkyB, will acquire a portion of News Corp's stake in the venture, bringing News Corp's ownership to 40 percent compared with 10 percent for MCI and 50 percent for EchoStar.
EchoStar, based in Englewood, Colorado, is a worldwide manufacturer and distributor of satellite TV products.
Officials with both companies said the alliance would enable the company to respond to the growing popularity for subscription television services, currently dominated by cable television operators.
"Our goal is not to be complimentary to cable, we want to eliminate cable," said Charles Ergen, chief executive officer of EchoStar.
The service is scheduled to begin delivering programs to U.S. households in early 1998.

Officials said the venture, which will operate under the Sky brand name, is expected to lose around $500 million in its first year but it should reach break-even by 1999 and generate more than $1 billion in operating cash flow by the year 2002.
News Corp. also controls British Sky Broadcasting, or BSkyB, Britain's leading pay-TV provider, and has a satellite TV joint venture in Japan, JSkyB, that is expected to begin full service next year.
"Jointly we will create a dynamic and promising new competitive force in the subscription marketplace," Murdoch said in a statement.
Unlike rival direct satellite providers, which are precluded from offering local programs, Sky expects to be able to offer both local programs and premium channels.

At first, the local programs will be available to 50 percent of American households, but by the end of next year the service area will be increased to 75 percent, creating a substantial competitor to cable operators and other satellite services.
"At that point, the cable guys will be calling for Dr. Kevorkian," Preston Padden, president of Worldwide Satellite Operations for News Corp. told reporters at a news conference here.
EchoStar plans to spin off some assets to shareholders, including its manufacturing an international businesses.
Under terms of the agreement, EchoStar's direct broadcast satellite business will remain in Englewood, Colo. Ergen will remain chief executive officer of EchoStar and Murdoch will become chairman.

The new Sky service is expected to include seven satellites, more than 500 channels, retransmission of local TV stations in markets representing more than 75 percent of all U.S. television households and low consumer entry cost.
ASkyB is currently building a multimillion-dollar broadcast facility in Gilbert, Ariz. to serve as its broadcast hub.
